Dungeons & Dragons maker will pass AI settlement money to authors | The Seattle Times

# Dungeons & Dragons maker will pass AI settlement money to authors 

 Nov. 27, 2026 at 6:00 am Updated Nov. 27, 2026 at 6:00 am 

By 

 Destiny Muller 

Seattle Times business reporter

Wizards of the Coast, the Renton-based maker of Dungeons & Dragons and Magic: The Gathering, is passing its portion of a massive copyright settlement with artificial intelligence company Anthropic to fantasy book authors.

The news surprised some authors, as the gamemaker could’ve kept the money. Authors began receiving letters last week announcing Wizards of the Coast’s decision, which stems from a broader class-action lawsuit that argued Anthropic violated copyright laws. 

Anthropic will pay $1.5 billion in total under the settlement, with payments due to authors, publishers and other copyright holders for roughly 400,000 to 500,000 works. 

The Wizards of the Coast books, which included novels, modules and stories, were written under work-for-hire contracts, so the company owned them outright. Authors were not entitled to the 50-50 author-publisher split outlined in the settlement.

“D&D wouldn’t be D&D without the creators who built its worlds,” Dan Ayoub, president of Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games, said in a statement to The Seattle Times about why the company wanted to give away its portion. Wizards of the Coast is a subsidiary of Hasbro.

About 400 Wizards of the Coast works are covered by the settlement, a company spokesperson said. Payouts will total about $3,000 per work. Those figures would put Wizards of the Coast’s share of the settlement at around $1.2 million, but the spokesperson declined to confirm that total.

A first installment of payments from Anthropic began going out the week of Nov. 23, the Authors Guild said. 

The settlement funds come from the Bartz v. Anthropic case, one of the first major lawsuits brought against an AI company for using unlicensed books to train large language models. 

In 2025, now retired U.S. District Judge William Alsup found that using books to train AI was fair use if they were acquired legally, but that Anthropic had illegally acquired pirated copies of books from the websites LibGen and PiLiMi.

Alsup’s ruling set the stage for a trial, but Anthropic instead reached a settlement with authors and publishers.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín gave the settlement final approval in July.

## ‘Unexpected gift’

“I was absolutely stunned,” said James Lowder, who has written D&D fiction since the early 1990s, when the books were published by TSR, which Wizards of the Coast later bought. He was among the first authors to get a letter about the settlement. He will be compensated for eight of his works, including five novels. 

King County-based author Mary Kirchoff also saw the payout as an “unexpected gift.” She started her career in the 1980s writing choose-your-own-adventure books for TSR. She now runs a children’s charity in Shoreline. Seven of her novels — some co-written — from her over 40-year career will be covered.

Unlike Lowder, Kirchoff didn’t file a claim in the suit. She held publishing leadership roles at TSR and later at Wizards of the Coast, and many of the early contracts were signed under her watch. She said she didn’t think she was owed anything because Wizards of the Coast controlled the copyrights to her work.

She understood why: The company needed to keep the copyrights so the shared worlds of its games would stay consistent, but the intention was always to welcome authors’ voices. 

“This one decision did more to honor that than anything I’ve witnessed in the interim,” Kirchoff said.

Kirchoff credited Lowder and bestselling author R.A. Salvatore with advocating for authors. Ayoub said the company decided from the start to share the settlement proceeds.

“I am thrilled to be working with a company that did the right thing,” Salvatore told The Times.

Asked whether Wizards of the Coast would hand over payouts from future AI-related lawsuits, the company spokesperson said, “We are focused on getting authors paid out under the Bartz matter. Beyond that, we don’t comment on litigation strategy.”

The spokesperson also pointed to March Hasbro guidelines that say the company doesn’t use its creative works to train AI without clear author permission.
